planting.note: Set out well after soil has warmed, since this compact golden-leaved selection sulks and drops foliage in cool, wet ground.

directions: This low, mounding sport of golden dewdrop holds bright chartreuse-gold foliage year-round with only sparse lavender-blue flowering, making it more of a foliage accent than a bloomer. Give it full sun for the deepest gold color; in shade the leaves fade toward green. Shear lightly two or three times a season to keep the mound dense, and protect from frost since dieback is common below the upper 20s F. It tolerates coastal heat and humidity well and works nicely as a low border or container specimen.

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger passes into a bed with sharp drainage, as this cultivar rots quickly in soggy winter soil.

directions: A free-flowering selection prized for its dense clusters of softly fragrant lavender-blue blooms that continue from spring through fall, followed by the species' typical golden berry clusters. Grow in full sun for the heaviest bud set and prune in late winter to shape, since flowers form on new growth. It is fast to reestablish from cuttings and makes a good informal hedge or butterfly-garden anchor along the Gulf Coast. Watch for whitefly on new flushes and treat promptly to keep foliage from yellowing.

planting.note: Install in spring against a wall or trellis to take advantage of reflected heat and to support its lax, sprawling stems.

directions: This white-flowered form of Cape plumbago produces the same clean phlox-like clusters as the species but in pure white rather than sky blue, brightening evening gardens and pairing well with blue-flowered companions. It shares the species' drought tolerance once established and its scrambling, semi-vining habit, so give it a fence, trellis, or slope to spill over. Cut back hard in late winter to remove cold-damaged wood and to encourage the flush of new growth that carries the summer bloom. It is slower to establish than the blue-flowered types and benefits from light feeding through the growing season.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set out in spring in a well-drained bed or large container; its tighter habit suits smaller Gulf Coast landscapes than the species.

directions: A dwarfed, denser-branching selection of Cape plumbago that stays low and mounding without the long scrambling canes of the species, making it useful for foundation plantings and mixed borders. Sky-blue flower clusters appear nearly continuously from late spring through fall in full sun. It needs less frequent pruning than standard Cape plumbago to stay tidy, though an annual late-winter cutback keeps it dense and floriferous. Established plants shrug off heat and short dry spells but appreciate deep watering during prolonged drought.

planting.note: Transplant after frost danger passes into rich, well-drained soil; stems are more upright than 'Black and Blue' but still benefit from a sheltered spot.

directions: This selection carries true cobalt-blue flower spikes without the dark calyces of 'Black and Blue', on a sturdier, less floppy plant that needs little staking. It flowers heavily from midsummer through frost and is a strong hummingbird draw along the Gulf Coast. Where winters dip into the mid-20s F the top growth dies back but the rootstock typically returns from a thick mulch layer. Pinch young plants once to encourage branching, and divide congested clumps every two to three years to maintain vigor.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant in spring once soil has warmed, spacing generously since this vigorous form spreads wider than typical anise sage cultivars.

directions: A robust, tall-growing anise sage selection with rich violet-purple flower spikes held on dark stems, offering more purple tone than the typical indigo-blue forms. It is vigorous enough to naturalize by rhizomes in warm climates, so give it room or plan to divide it periodically. Full sun to light afternoon shade produces the heaviest bloom, while afternoon shade in the Deep South helps foliage stay fresh through peak summer heat. Cut stems back hard after a killing frost and mulch the crown; regrowth is reliable in zone 8 and warmer.
